lesson.title: What a Z-Score Is Really Telling You
lesson.summary: Interpreting a z-score means reading both its sign and its size to judge how typical or unusual a value is, and for roughly normal distributions, connecting specific z-scores to specific percentiles.
lesson.body:
Calculating a z-score is only half the job; the more valuable skill is reading what that number tells you about a value's place in its distribution. The sign tells you direction: a positive z-score means the value lies above the mean, a negative z-score means it lies below the mean, and a z-score of exactly 0 means the value equals the mean. The size, or magnitude, tells you how far that value is from typical: a z-score near 0 describes an ordinary, unremarkable value, while a z-score far from 0 in either direction describes a value that stands out.

A commonly used rule of thumb treats z-scores beyond positive or negative 2 as moderately unusual and z-scores beyond positive or negative 3 as very unusual, though the exact cutoff depends on context and on the shape of the distribution. This rule of thumb connects most precisely to distributions that are approximately bell shaped, because for such distributions there are well established percentages of data that fall within each standard deviation of the mean.

Take the z-score of 1.5 calculated in the previous section, for a test score of 650 on a test with mean 500 and standard deviation 100. If this test's scores follow an approximately normal distribution, a standard normal table shows that about 93.3 percent of values fall at or below a z-score of 1.5. So this student's score is not just above average, it outperforms roughly 93 percent of test takers, placing the student near the top of the distribution. Compare this to the z-score of negative 2 calculated for a raw score of 300 on the same test: a standard normal table shows only about 2.3 percent of values fall at or below a z-score of negative 2, meaning a score of 300 is quite unusual, near the bottom of the distribution.

It is worth being careful here: connecting a specific z-score to a specific percentile this precisely only works when the underlying distribution is approximately normal. A z-score still tells you distance from the mean in standard deviation units for any distribution, symmetric or skewed, but the exact percentage of data below a given z-score can differ substantially in a skewed distribution. This is the same caution that applies to the mean and standard deviation themselves: since neither is resistant, a skewed distribution or an outlier can produce misleading z-scores even when the arithmetic is done correctly.

Reading z-scores well means always asking two questions together: which direction, and how far. A z-score of positive 0.3 and a z-score of positive 3.0 are both above average, but they describe very different levels of unusualness, one barely distinguishable from typical, the other extremely rare. This combination of direction and magnitude is what makes the z-score such a compact, information dense way to describe a single value's position within its distribution.
